title: Use of AI by Dutch businesses has more than doubled
content:
Use of AI by business has more than doubled, largest increase seen in SMEs
In 2026, 41 percent of enterprises with ten or more workers used one or more types of AI technologies, more than twice as many as in 2025. Enterprises are using more artificial intelligence above all for marketing or sales. The use of AI increased the most in the areas of accounting, auditing and financial management. Self-employed people mainly use AI to search for information and for writing. This is according to recent figures on the use of ICT by companies from Statistics Netherlands (CBS).
Both small and larger enterprises are using more artificial intelligence. The increase is the most pronounced among SMEs (between 2 and 249 employees). The use of AI is the most widespread among larger enterprises.
Use of text generation has seen a particular increase
The AI technologies most commonly used by enterprises are natural language generation (generating written or spoken language or code: 28 percent), text mining (the analysis of written text: 24 percent) and creating images, videos or audio files (24 percent). The use of natural language has increased by the most, from 8 percent in 2025 to 28 percent in 2026.
Use of AI is highest in information and communication, and lowest in the construction sector
Enterprises in the information and communication sector were the most likely to use one or more types of AI technologies, at 80 percent (compared to 59 percent in 2025). Publishing companies and media organisations also use AI frequently: 75 percent (42 percent in 2025). More than half of enterprises in the specialised business services and real estate activities sectors were using at least one type of AI technology in 2026. 
AI use is lowest in the construction sector, accommodation and food services, and the transportation and storage sector. The increase was the most pronounced – a fourfold rise – among enterprises in the accommodation and food services sector and in transportation and storage.
AI use in accounting, auditing and financial management has doubled
Among enterprises that use AI-based software or systems, 42 percent do so for marketing or sales purposes. 35 percent of enterprises use AI for business administration or management tasks (such as risk assessment, selecting job applicants, basic translations or planning) and 30 percent for accounting, auditing and financial management. 
The increase in AI use is most pronounced in accounting, auditing and financial management: from 17 percent in 2025 to 30 percent in 2026. Only 6 percent of enterprises use AI for logistics purposes.
Productivity increase in over half of enterprises
54 percent of enterprises using one or more types of AI technologies said that the use of AI has led to a productivity increase. 30 percent indicated that the nature of their work has changed as a result of AI. Another 16 percent of enterprises said that fewer staff are required, and 4 percent indicated that new roles and jobs are being created due to the use of AI use. A quarter say that it has had no impact on their company.
6 in 10 self-employed people use AI
Around 60 percent of self-employed workers without staff (ZZP) occasionally use AI, particularly to look up information or ask questions (54 percent). This group is the least likely to use AI to develop software or writing programme code (8 percent), or to communicate with customers (9 percent).
Sources
- StatLine - ICT use in small businesses (in Dutch)
- StatLine - ICT use among self-employed workers without staff

report.summary: CBS data show Dutch enterprise AI use more than doubled to 41% in 2026, led by SMEs and text-generation tools.
report.background: The Netherlands has a highly digital economy, but enterprise AI adoption started from a low base. The 2025 CBS survey showed relatively limited use outside tech-heavy sectors; by 2026, generative AI tools had become more accessible, cheaper and embedded in common business software. That shift helped smaller firms catch up, especially in marketing, administration and finance. The data comes from Statistics Netherlands' ICT-use survey, which covers enterprises with ten or more workers and self-employed people without staff. It measures self-reported use of technologies such as natural-language generation, text mining and media creation, not the depth or sophistication of deployment. Sector differences remain stark: information and communication firms lead, while construction, hospitality and transport lag, although some low-adoption sectors recorded the fastest relative growth.
key_points: Overall adoption reached 41% of enterprises with ten or more workers in 2026, more than double the 2025 level. Small and medium-sized enterprises recorded the largest increase, while larger firms still have the highest adoption rate. The figures suggest AI is moving from experimental pilots into mainstream business use.

Natural-language generation became the most common AI technology, rising from 8% in 2025 to 28% in 2026. Text mining and image, video or audio creation followed at 24% each. The surge points to growing use of generative AI for writing, code and content production rather than only data analysis.

Sector adoption varies widely. Information and communication enterprises reached 80%, and publishing and media organisations 75%. Construction, accommodation and food services, and transportation and storage had the lowest use, but hospitality and transport saw a fourfold relative increase, showing diffusion beyond tech hubs.

Among AI-using enterprises, 42% apply it to marketing or sales, 35% to business administration or management, and 30% to accounting, auditing and financial management. Accounting use rose from 17% to 30%, while logistics remained low at 6%. This suggests back-office finance is becoming a key AI entry point.

Just over half of AI-using enterprises, 54%, reported a productivity increase. 30% said the nature of their work changed, 16% needed fewer staff, and 4% created new roles; a quarter saw no impact. Separately, about 60% of self-employed people use AI, mainly to find information or ask questions.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the Dutch data confirm that demand is broadening beyond early adopters into SMEs and back-office functions such as accounting and administration. That favours vendors offering affordable, integrated and Dutch- or EU-language-capable tools, plus governance features for privacy and compliance. For developers, the opportunity is less about building another chatbot and more about workflow integration, evaluation, data controls and vertical applications. For regular users, AI will increasingly appear inside marketing, finance and admin software rather than as a standalone product. The productivity findings are self-reported and not causal, so businesses should measure results carefully. Workers should also expect task changes and need basic AI literacy, while job losses appear limited so far in the survey.
report.tools: To follow the trend, watch Microsoft 365 Copilot, ChatGPT, Google Gemini and Claude for SME-ready productivity. Open-source options include Ollama for local models, Hugging Face Transformers, LangChain for workflows, and Llama or Mistral models for privacy-sensitive deployments. For Dutch data, use CBS StatLine; for compliance, track EU AI Act guidance.
